title: From Speculation to Science: How Do People Learn?
author: Terry U
summary: This comprehensive essay synthesizes decades of learning science research to argue that American teacher preparation and school practice remain largely divorced from what neuroscience and cognitive psychology reveal about how humans learn. Terry traces the evolution from speculation through behaviorism to modern cognitive science, highlighting three foundational principles: students arrive with preconceptions that filter new information; deep understanding requires knowledge organized around concepts and conditionalized for application; and metacognition—learning how to learn—must be explicitly taught. The essay documents how school segregation undermined these principles and argues that current LLM disruption exposes the bankruptcy of transmission-model teaching. Teachers need rigorous preparation grounded in learning science.
points: Learning science is real science: Like climate science or epidemiology, learning science has accumulated decades of rigorous research with direct policy implications that are systematically ignored by American education.

Preconceptions filter all new learning: Students don't receive information passively; they filter everything through existing mental models. Teachers must surface and engage misconceptions rather than simply explain correct answers.

Deep understanding requires knowledge architecture: Experts organize knowledge around principles and conditions of applicability. Curricula that prioritize breadth over depth prevent the deep, connected understanding that distinguishes competence.

Segregation reversed learning gains: Integration in the 1970s-80s narrowed achievement gaps by changing belonging, reducing stereotype threat, and diversifying peer learning. Post-1988 resegregation reversed all gains, proving culture and context matter profoundly.

LLMs expose transmission teaching as hollow: The machine's ability to produce correct outputs without understanding reveals that schools trained mimicry, not thinking. Teachers grounded in learning science are unafraid of AI.
quotes: Learning: From Speculation to Science.' The report opens with a striking claim: 'The world is in the midst of an extraordinary outpouring of scientific work on the mind and brain...
Students come to the classroom with preconceptions about how the world works. If their initial understanding is not surfaced, they may fail to grasp new concepts and information.

Experts don't just know more than novices—their knowledge is structured differently. Knowledge isn't useful unless it's organized, connected, and tagged with information about when and where it applies.
The science of learning tells us that teachers must understand each child's prior knowledge, cultural tools, and ways of making meaning. This is the central challenge.

Integrated classrooms fostered belonging, reduced stereotype threat, diversified peer learning, and forced teachers to recognize that children who spoke and reasoned differently weren't deficient, just different.” Archived from Terry U on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
